analogy.p: Think of the live wire as the high-pressure water main, the neutral as the return drain, and the earth wire as an emergency overflow pipe that is always closed in normal use. If a fault allows the high-pressure water to leak into the metal casing, the overflow pipe lets a large flow escape, and that rush of water trips a cut-off valve (the fuse) that shuts the supply off. The analogy breaks down because water pressure is not an alternating push, and a real fuse melts and must be replaced, whereas a cut-off valve could just be reset.
analogy.t: A garden hose with a safety valve

bullets: The copper cores are chosen because copper is a good **conductor** and is flexible.
Each core has plastic insulation of a standard colour so that the plug can be wired correctly.
The outer sheath holds the three wires together and adds extra insulation and strength.
Together the live and neutral wires carry the current to and from the appliance in normal use.
The earth wire is a **safety wire**: it does not normally carry current.
A **two-core cable** (live and neutral only) is used for appliances with plastic casings, which are double insulated.
The mains plug connects the three wires to the three pins that push into the socket.
Link to topics: a.c. and d.c., power (P = I V), and the National Grid.
core.h: Mains electricity and the three-core cable
core.p: Mains electricity in the UK is an **alternating potential difference of about 230 V at 50 Hz** (see the d.c. and a.c. topic). Most electrical appliances are connected to the mains using a **three-core cable**. This is a cable containing three separate copper wires (cores), each covered by its own coloured plastic insulation, with a strong outer plastic sheath around all three. The plastic is an electrical insulator, so it stops the current flowing out of the wires and protects the user from shock. The three wires have different jobs and different p.d.s: the **live wire**, the **neutral wire** and the **earth wire**.

bullets: Colour: **brown**.
P.d. between live and earth: about **230 V** (a.c.).
The live wire is the one that connects to the **fuse** and the **switch** in a properly wired appliance.
The fuse is wired into the live side of the plug so that, when it melts, the appliance is disconnected from the high p.d.
Switches are also placed in the live wire; if they were in the neutral wire the appliance would stay connected to 230 V even when off.
In the UK plug the live wire connects to the terminal on the right (looking inside with the cable at the bottom) which is joined to the fuse and then the live pin.
A 230 V mains supply is far higher than the p.d. of a cell (1.5 V), which is why it is so dangerous.
core.p: The **live wire** has **brown** insulation. It carries the alternating p.d. from the supply, which is about **230 V** relative to earth. Because the live wire is at a high p.d. compared with earth, it is the dangerous wire: if you touch it while you are in contact with the ground, a current will flow through your body. Its p.d. alternates between positive and negative values 50 times every second. The live wire is the wire that brings the energy to the appliance.

bullets: Colour: **blue**.
P.d. between neutral and earth: about **0 V**.
Function: **completes the circuit** so that a current can flow through the appliance.
Normally carries the same size of current as the live wire, but in the opposite sense.
Neutral is connected to the earth at the local substation, which is why its p.d. relative to earth is about zero.
The p.d. across the appliance is the p.d. between the live and neutral wires, about 230 V.
No fuse or switch is put in the neutral wire in a domestic plug.
core.p: The **neutral wire** has **blue** insulation. Its job is to **complete the circuit**: current flows in through the live wire, through the appliance, and back out through the neutral wire (and, because the supply is alternating, the directions reverse 50 times a second). The neutral wire is kept at about **0 V**, because it is connected to earth at the electricity substation. Because it is at about 0 V relative to earth, it is not dangerous in the same way as the live wire, although you should still treat the whole cable as dangerous.

bullets: Colour: **green and yellow stripes**.
Function: a **safety wire** that stops the appliance casing from becoming live.
It carries a current **only if there is a fault**.
It is connected to the **metal casing** (and any exposed metal parts).
It has a very **low resistance** so a large current flows if a fault occurs.
In the plug it is connected to the **earth pin**, which is the longest pin and opens the shutters on the socket.
Not needed in a double-insulated appliance because there is no exposed metal to become live.
core.h: The earth wire (green and yellow stripes)
core.p: The **earth wire** has **green and yellow stripes** and is at **0 V**. It is a safety wire. In normal use it **does not carry any current**. It is connected to the metal casing of the appliance (and to any other exposed metal that could become live). Its job is to **stop the casing becoming live** and to allow a **large current to flow to earth** if there is a fault, so that the fuse melts and the appliance is disconnected. It only carries a current when there is a fault.

bullets: An **open switch** only isolates the part of the circuit after the switch from the supply; the live wire before the switch is still at 230 V.
The p.d. between **live and earth** is about 230 V, so a current flows if a person makes a connection.
The human body conducts electricity, especially when wet (low resistance), so a larger current flows.
The current through the body can cause **heart fibrillation**, burns and muscle spasms; even small currents can be dangerous.
Neutral and earth are at about 0 V so touching them alone gives no large p.d.
That is why you should **unplug** an appliance before repairing it and never touch bare wires.
Switches and fuses are placed in the **live** wire so the appliance is disconnected from the 230 V when they are open or melted.
core.h: Why the live wire is dangerous even if the switch is open
core.p: The specification states that the live wire may be **dangerous even when a switch in the mains circuit is open**. A switch (or fuse) only breaks the circuit in one place; it does not remove the p.d. from the rest of the wire. If the switch is in the live wire and is open, the live wire on the **supply side** of the switch (leading back to the supply) remains at about 230 V relative to earth. A person who touches that part of the live wire while standing on the ground (or touching earthed metal such as a pipe) provides a path to earth. A current flows through the person's body because there is a p.d. of 230 V between the live wire and earth, and this can cause serious injury or death.

bullets: Step 1: **a fault** - the live wire touches the metal case.
Step 2: the case is connected to the **earth wire**, a **low resistance** path to earth.
Step 3: a **large current** flows from live through the case and out through the earth wire.
Step 4: the large current **heats the thin fuse wire** until it **melts** (the fuse 'blows').
Step 5: the **circuit is broken**, so the live wire is **disconnected** from the appliance.
Step 6: the case is **no longer live**, so it is **safe to touch**.
Key words for the mark scheme: **earth wire**, **large current**, **fuse melts/blows**, **circuit broken / live disconnected**.
Without the earth wire, the fuse would not blow and the case would stay live.
core.h: How the earth wire and fuse protect the user (the 4-mark explanation)
core.p: This is the most commonly examined explanation in the topic. Suppose a fault allows the **live wire to touch the metal case** of an appliance, such as a toaster. Without protection, the case would become live at 230 V and anyone touching it would get a shock. With the **earth wire** connected to the case, a **very large current** flows from the live wire, through the case and along the low-resistance earth wire to earth. This large current makes the **fuse wire heat up and melt**, which **breaks the circuit** and **disconnects the live wire** from the appliance. The case can then no longer become live, so the user is protected.

bullets: Typical household fuse ratings are **3 A, 5 A and 13 A**.
Choose the **next fuse rating above** the normal current drawn by the appliance.
Normal current can be found from **I = P / V** (power divided by p.d.), using V = 230 V.
Example: a 2300 W kettle draws I = 2300 / 230 = **10 A**, so a **13 A** fuse is used.
Example: a 60 W lamp draws about 0.26 A so a **3 A** fuse is used.
A fuse must be **replaced** after it blows once the fault is fixed; it cannot be reset.
A **circuit breaker** (an electromagnetic switch) does the same job as a fuse but can be **reset** and acts faster.
The fuse protects the **wiring and appliance from overheating and fire** as well as the user.
core.h: Fuses: how they work and choosing the rating
core.p: A **fuse** is a safety device containing a thin wire that melts if the current becomes too large. The wire has a **resistance** so a current heats it, and if the current exceeds the **fuse rating** the wire melts and breaks the circuit. The rating of the fuse is the maximum current it allows before it melts. For a safe design the rating should be **just above** the normal working current of the appliance: too low and it blows in normal use, too high and it will not protect the appliance and wires because a fault current could be too high without melting the fuse.

bullets: Earth (green/yellow) -> top pin (longest).
Neutral (blue) -> left pin (looking from the back with the cable at the bottom).
Live (brown) -> right pin, through the fuse.
Only a small length of bare wire should show at each terminal; **no loose strands** can touch other terminals.
Wires should be firmly screwed in so they cannot work loose, which could cause a fault.
The outer sheath should be clamped by the **cable grip** so the wires are not pulled out.
The **casing is plastic** so the plug cannot become live.
If a plug is wrongly wired (for example live and neutral swapped), the appliance may still work but its fuse and switch would be in the neutral wire, so the appliance is not safely isolated.
core.p: A UK three-pin plug has a **plastic casing** (an insulator, so it is safe to hold) and **brass pins** (brass is a good conductor and does not corrode). Inside the plug each wire connects to the matching terminal: the **brown live wire** to the live terminal (next to the fuse), the **blue neutral wire** to the neutral terminal and the **green and yellow earth wire** to the earth terminal at the top. The **cable grip** clamps the outer insulation (sheath) so that strain on the cable pulls on the grip and not on the wires.

bullets: Plastic is an **insulator**; metal is a **conductor**.
Double-insulated appliances are marked with a square within a square symbol.
They have no earth wire because there is no conducting casing that could become live.
Appliances with metal cases (kettle, toaster, cooker, washing machine) **must be earthed**.
The earth wire is connected to the casing so it is held at 0 V.
Both types still need a **fuse** in the live wire.
core.p: Some appliances, such as hairdryers and many lamps, have a **plastic casing** and are described as **double insulated**. The casing is an electrical insulator, so even if the live wire came loose inside, the user could not touch a live metal part. These appliances use a **two-core cable** (live and neutral only) and do not need an earth wire. Metal-cased appliances, such as kettles, toasters and washing machines, must be earthed because metal is a good conductor.

bullets: **Frayed or damaged insulation** can expose the live wire, so touching it completes a circuit to earth.
**Water** lowers the resistance of the body and can make electrical contact between the live wire and earth, so keep mains devices away from water (for example bathrooms).
**Overloading a socket** (plugging in too many appliances) draws a large current which heats the cable and can start a fire.
Long **extension leads** should be fully unwound when carrying a large current to avoid overheating.
Always **switch off and unplug** before changing a bulb or repairing an appliance.
Never use a fuse with a **rating that is too high**, or replace it with a nail or foil, because then it will not blow.
**Do not push objects into sockets**; the shutters are opened only by the longer earth pin.
core.h: Safe and dangerous practices around mains
core.p: Many mains accidents happen through damaged cables, wet conditions and misuse. Knowing why each hazard is dangerous links the physics (a p.d. between live and earth, and a path for current) to everyday behaviour. These ideas are often asked as 'explain why' questions.

bullets: **I = V / R:** a low-resistance earth path gives a large fault current.
**Heating effect of current:** the fuse wire has resistance, so a large current transfers a lot of energy as thermal energy and melts it.
**P = I V:** used to calculate the normal current and choose the fuse rating.
**National Grid:** the mains is delivered at 230 V by step-down transformers; the neutral is earthed at the substation.
**Series/parallel circuits:** the fuse and switch are connected in **series** with the appliance.
**Resistance and body:** wet skin has a lower resistance so a larger current flows through the body.
**Energy and power ratings:** appliances with a higher power rating draw a larger current and need a higher-rated fuse.
core.h: Link to other topics and Higher-level reasoning
core.p: This topic builds on current, p.d., resistance and power, and it links to the National Grid. A good answer uses the physics: the earth wire has low resistance so a fault current is large (I = V / R); the fuse wire heats because of the current heating effect; the energy is transferred as thermal energy (P = I squared R). Being able to link these makes 6-mark answers much stronger.

exam: **Recall (1 mark each):** live = brown, neutral = blue, earth = green and yellow stripes; live about 230 V, neutral and earth about 0 V.
**Function marks:** live carries the alternating p.d. from the supply; neutral completes the circuit; earth is a safety wire that only carries a current if there is a fault.

**4-mark fault explanation:** (1) live wire touches the metal case, (2) a large current flows through the earth wire, (3) the fuse melts, (4) the circuit is broken / live disconnected so the case is safe.
**Always say** 'large current' and 'fuse melts' or 'blows' - not just 'the fuse trips' or 'cuts off'.
**Why in the live wire?** So that when the fuse blows or switch opens, the appliance is disconnected from the 230 V; in the neutral wire it would still be live.
**Fuse choice (3 marks):** I = P / V (1), substitute with correct units (1), choose the fuse rating just above the calculated current (1).
**Open switch question:** state that there is still a p.d. of about 230 V between the live wire and earth, so a current can flow through a person touching it.
**Plug questions:** plastic casing (insulator), brass pins (good conductor), cable grip holds the sheath; name each wire and where it connects.
**6-mark questions:** link the physics - low resistance of the earth wire, large current, heating effect melts fuse, circuit broken.
**Avoid** vague words such as 'electricity goes to the ground' or 'shock'; use 'current flows through the person to earth' and 'potential difference'.

mistakes.r: The earth wire carries a current only if there is a fault.
mistakes.w: The earth wire carries current all the time.

mistakes.r: The large current makes the fuse wire melt, which breaks the circuit and disconnects the live wire.
mistakes.w: The fuse stops the electricity so the user is safe.

mistakes.r: The neutral wire is at about 0 V; the live wire is at about 230 V.
mistakes.w: The neutral wire is at 230 V.

mistakes.r: Live is brown, neutral is blue, earth is green and yellow stripes.
mistakes.w: Live is blue and neutral is brown.

mistakes.r: The live wire can still be dangerous when a switch is open because there is a p.d. between the live wire and earth.
mistakes.w: The live wire is safe when the switch is off.

mistakes.r: The fuse (and switch) are in the live wire so the appliance is disconnected from 230 V.
mistakes.w: The fuse goes in the neutral wire.

mistakes.r: Use a fuse rating just above the normal current; too large a rating will not protect the appliance.
mistakes.w: Use a 13 A fuse for everything to be safe.

mistakes.r: The earth wire stops the casing becoming live and provides a low-resistance path to earth if there is a fault.
mistakes.w: The earth wire stops the current from entering the appliance.

mistakes.r: You are at risk when you touch the live wire and provide a path to earth.
mistakes.w: Electricity is only dangerous if you touch the wire and the neutral.

summary: The specification asks you to know that most appliances are connected to the mains by a three-core cable containing the live (brown), neutral (blue) and earth (green and yellow stripes) wires, their potentials and functions, and why the live wire can still be dangerous when a switch is open. It matters because mains-safety questions (wiring a plug, explaining how the earth wire and fuse protect the user) are a frequent 4-6 mark Paper 1 question.

terms.d: The wire (brown) that carries the alternating p.d. of about 230 V from the supply to the appliance.
The wire (blue) that completes the circuit; it is at about 0 V.
The safety wire (green and yellow stripes) at 0 V; it only carries a current if there is a fault.
A cable containing the live, neutral and earth wires, each with its own insulation, inside an outer sheath.
A safety device containing a thin wire that melts if the current exceeds its rating, breaking the circuit.
The maximum current a fuse will allow before it melts; chosen just above the normal current of the appliance.
An electromagnetic switch that opens automatically when the current is too large and can be reset.
The energy transferred per unit charge between two points; measured in volts (V).
A material that does not allow current to flow through it, such as plastic.
A material that allows current to flow through it easily, such as copper or brass.
Connecting the metal casing of an appliance to the ground (0 V) through the earth wire so it cannot become live.
An appliance with a plastic casing so that the user cannot touch live parts; it does not need an earth wire.
A failure in an appliance, for example when the live wire touches the metal casing.
A clamp in a plug that holds the outer sheath of the cable so the wires are not pulled out of their terminals.
Drawing too large a current from a socket by connecting too many appliances, which can overheat the cables.

worked.ans: Normal current = 10 A; use the 13 A fuse.
worked.q: A kettle is rated at 2300 W and is connected to the 230 V mains. Fuses of 3 A, 5 A and 13 A are available. Calculate the normal current and choose the correct fuse. (4 marks)
steps: The fuse must be just above 10 A: the 3 A and 5 A fuses would melt in normal use.
The 13 A fuse is the smallest rating above 10 A.

worked.ans: Current = 0.26 A; use the 3 A fuse.
worked.q: A table lamp is rated at 60 W and is connected to the 230 V mains. Fuses of 3 A, 5 A and 13 A are available. Which fuse should be used? (3 marks)
steps: The fuse rating should be just above this current: 3 A is the smallest available.

worked.ans: Earth wire gives a low-resistance path so a large current flows; the fuse melts, breaking the circuit and disconnecting the live wire, so the case is safe to touch.
worked.q: A toaster has a metal case. Explain how the earth wire and the fuse protect the user if the live wire becomes loose and touches the case. (4 marks)
steps: The earth wire is connected to the metal case.
A large current flows through the earth wire (low resistance path to earth) when the live wire touches the case.
The large current makes the fuse wire heat up and melt.
This breaks the circuit and disconnects the live wire, so the case cannot become live.
